title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
description: Georgia state Rep. Carolyn Hugley, the p
body:
Georgia state Rep. Carolyn Hugley, the party's nominee for speaker of the state House, speaks in front of members of the Democratic caucus Thursday in the capitol.
                
                    Sarah Kallis/GPB News
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sarah Kallis/GPB News
    

   
   The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.   Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years. The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years.   The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.   Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18. The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided.    
   So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.   The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.   New Democratic 'trifectas,'  controlling the legislature and governor's office   The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.   The president of their rival organization, Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."   
   Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."   In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.   One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program, which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.   
   In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.   Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.   Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.)   Democrats can break Republican momentum in some states   In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.   Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.   Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.   North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.   In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.   
   That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.      Colin Campbell of WUNC, Sarah Kallis of Georgia Public Broadcasting, Carmen Russell-Sluchansky of WHYY and Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ, contributed to this story.

title: Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case
description:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., on his challenge for Senate majority leader
    
        
                Download
body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., on his challenge for Senate majority leader
    
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6041687/nx-s1-10006246" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during the What's Next summit in Denver on Friday.
                
                    Mark Makela/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Makela/Getty Images
    

   
   Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.   "Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen told NPR's Steve Inskeep on Morning Edition.   Over the weekend, he appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News to make his case for new Democratic leadership after his party's sweeping midterm victories. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, says he has enough votes to remain leader.   
   Van Hollen is hardly a Washington outsider. The progressive Democrat has spent nearly 25 years on Capitol Hill, served as a deputy to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and led Democratic campaign efforts in both chambers. He has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, and he has called for investigations into the administration's foreign aid cuts.   Schumer has continued to support U.S. military assistance to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Van Hollen, by contrast, has pushed to restrict weapons sales and military aid to the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, while pressing for more humanitarian aid to Palestinians.   "I certainly oppose the idea of an American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel, regardless of its actions," Van Hollen said.   Van Hollen also wants Democratic leaders to stay out of contested primaries. He pointed to the victories of incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.   "We have two senators-elect who would not be there if the current majority leader had his way," he said.   He described the midterm victories as a populist rejection of President Trump, rather than an election orchestrated by Washington Democrats.   
   Van Hollen also cited legislation to strengthen labor unions, which never received a vote on the Senate floor. On the war in Iran, he called for an end to further funding.   "We should not be voting for one penny in mid-December to continue this war," he said.   Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win. The election will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, making it difficult to know how many votes either candidate secured.   Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.   The digital version of this live interview was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: FAA ground stop still affecting thousands of flights. And, Trump meets Xi, Putin in Asia
description:
FAA Ground Stop Update, Democratic Leadership Contest, Trump's Travels To Asia
    
            
                
                Transc
body:
FAA Ground Stop Update, Democratic Leadership Contest, Trump's Travels To Asia
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-153841/nx-s1-mx-6042207-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Travelers are expected to face continued disruptions at airports as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide ground stop. As of Sunday evening, more than 2,300 flights have been canceled, and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed, according to FlightAware.com. Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta airports saw the most disruptions, with over 250 delayed flights each. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, was doing routine maintenance in at least one remote location, changing copper wire to fiber optics.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Aircraft are seen at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide.
                
                    Tom Brenner/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/AP
    

   
   🎧 The U.S. air traffic system remains safe, and this recent incident is considered an unusual meltdown, NPR's Joel Rose tells Up First. The Federal Aviation Administration believes it has identified the issue, and airlines will be ready for the holiday travel rush. Rose says the nation's air traffic system has suffered from decades of underinvestment by Congress and administrations from both parties. Before the ground stop, Duffy had requested $30 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. Now he seems to be asking for $50 billion by the end of the year, on top of the $12.5 billion for air traffic equipment that the Trump administration secured from Congress last year. Democrats, who will control Congress in January, are not responding positively to Duffy's latest request. Rose expects Democrats to seek more clarity on the administration's spending and the causes of the ground stop.   
   As Democrats gear up for substantial majorities in Congress, one question looms: who will take the helm? So far, no one has challenged Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for the House speaker role. Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is setting his sights on unseating longtime leader Chuck Schumer in the Senate.   🎧 A wave of incoming senators has spent months hearing voters demand change in Washington. NPR's Eric McDaniel says this presents a real opportunity for Van Hollen and a potential risk for Schumer, especially after the recent election results. Van Hollen needs 30 Democrats to secure a simple majority. He has support he needs from popular progressives like Bernie Sanders, and incoming members like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, McDaniel says. Since votes are cast by secret ballot, it's uncertain how many will back each leader when they convene in a few weeks, and McDaniel says anything could happen.   President Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this morning for a high-profile trip, which includes a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This marks Trump's second visit to China this year. The trip to Asia comes as the administration faces scrutiny following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman linked to China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. He traveled to China with Trump earlier this year; this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is accompanying Trump to Shenzhen.   
   🎧 It's not unusual for presidents who face midterm election defeats to shift their focus to foreign policy, NPR's Mara Liasson says. But Trump's recent foreign policy efforts, including tariffs and the war in Iran, have been widely unpopular and seen as reasons why his party lost in the midterms, Liasson says. The White House said that Trump isn't expected to address pressing issues like the war in Ukraine or tensions with China during this trip. Instead, he plans to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons. Trump will also skip mentioning Huang's affair. Bringing up the Nvidia situation could serve as a reminder that many in Congress believe the U.S. should restrict access to advanced chips in China. Trump disagrees with Congress on the matter, likely due to his ties with Huang, who committed millions of dollars for Trump's ballroom, Liasson says.   Living better   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Woman with insomnia
                
                    Mono/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mono/Getty Images
    

   
   Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.   Sleep plays a crucial role in weight management. Studies have found that poor sleep can increase appetite and lead to overeating, making it harder to shed pounds. On the flip side, quality sleep might actually enhance your weight-loss efforts. One study found that participants in a year-long weight-loss program who enjoyed better sleep lost more weight and fat. So, prioritizing sleep could be your secret weapon in the journey to a healthy weight. Here's what researchers say:   😴 While evidence linking more sleep to weight loss is limited, there is consistent science connecting insufficient sleep to weight gain.😴 Lack of sleep increases activity in brain regions associated with pleasure and reward, making it harder to make good food choices.😴 Not having enough sleep can disrupt circadian rhythms and reduce insulin sensitivity, encouraging fat storage and weight gain.😴 The relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. Eating added sugars and saturated fats disrupts sleep and reduces deep sleep, while consuming fruits, vegetables and fiber improves sleep quality and decreases nighttime awakenings.   
   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A "Route 66" sign is painted on the asphalt near Amboy in the Mojave Desert in California on Feb. 27, 2019.
                
                    Eric Baradat/AFP via Getty Images
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Eric Baradat/AFP via Getty Images

   
   Route 66 is celebrating an incredible century as America's most iconic highway. Stretching across eight states — from the vibrant streets of Chicago to the sun-soaked shores of Santa Monica, Calif. — this legendary route invites you to embrace the spirit of adventure on the open road. Imagine cruising through vast plains, rolling prairies, stunning canyons and shimmering deserts. Along the way, you'll discover a mix of big cities, charming cow towns and ghost towns. Over the decades, Route 66 has inspired countless songs, been captured in books, been seen in artwork and been celebrated in Pixar's 2006 animated movie Cars. So hop in, buckle up and experience the magic of Route 66 through these photos.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This illustration provided by NASA depicts Voyager 1.
                
                    AP/NASA
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        AP/NASA
    

   
   NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any human-launched object and is about to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that's one light-day away from Earth.New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River. They are seeking at least $1 million in damages.Mauricio Pochettino, who guided the U.S. men's national soccer team to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is leaving to become the head coach of Manchester United in the English Premier League.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Affordability was a key issue for midterm voters. It helped make childcare one, too
description: A toddler plays hide and seek with her p
body:
A toddler plays hide and seek with her parents as they cast their ballots at Valley Bible Chalet on Nov. 3 in Indian, Alaska.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   As affordability soared to the top of voters' minds going into the midterms, it helped elevate an issue that advocates say has often been on the fringes of mainstream political debate: childcare.   There were gubernatorial hopefuls who won their elections while running on promises to expand statewide childcare initiatives. New Mexico's Democratic Governor-elect Deb Haaland, for example, vowed to expand the state's first-of-its-kind universal childcare program. Some incoming members of Congress stressed the need for affordable childcare on the stump, such as South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who is also set to become the first pediatrician to serve in the Senate.   
   It wasn't just politicians; voters expressed their support for childcare, too. Electorates from Baltimore to San Antonio approved ballot measures that would see their tax dollars spent on local childcare initiatives.   "This election in particular really felt different," said Julie Kashen, founder and principal of the initiative Women's Economic Futures. "This felt like a real momentum moment for childcare as an election issue."   Childcare costs have surged in recent years, with the average annual cost topping $13,000 last year, according to the group Child Care Aware of America. It's putting a major financial burden on American families. A poll released by the First Five Years Fund in July found that 38% of parents who paid for childcare listed it as one of their top two financial concerns, behind only housing and groceries.   
   During the latest election cycle, politicians responded. Three quarters of gubernatorial candidates in the midterms offered policy proposals or took positions on childcare, including both Democrats and Republicans, according to data compiled by the Bank Street College of Education. The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy PAC, which advocates for more affordable caregiving policies, said it spent more than $40 million in competitive races across the country.   Melissa Boteach, chief policy officer of the nonprofit Zero to Three, which advocates for young children and their families, said more people have come to see childcare as not just a personal family struggle but also a systemic social concern. "Twenty years ago, this was more of an outside, on-the-margins issue," she said. "People have realized that this is a collective problem and that only collective action will solve it."   
   Kashen noted that the U.S. government has made major national investments in childcare before, such as in World War II and again during the COVID pandemic, when lockdowns sent the childcare sector into disarray. That recent disruption plus continued political organizing had helped boost the issue in the public consciousness, she added.   "What we're seeing now is the momentum over those years," Kashen said.   How childcare issues fared in the midterms   That shifting public understanding of childcare was borne out in cities and towns across the U.S. in recent months. In Washington, D.C., where childcare had long been a part of the political conversation, "the election took it to the next level," said Ruqiyyah Anbar-Shaheen, director of early childhood systems at DC Action, an advocacy organization focused on kids and families.   D.C. Democratic Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George ran on a promise to cap childcare costs at 7% of household income and support the Early Childhood Educator Pay Equity Fund, a municipal program intended to raise the pay of childcare workers that has been the target of proposed funding cuts.   "It's the first time we've seen childcare elevated to that level in a very long time in D.C.," Anbar-Shaheen said.   Childcare came up in competitive Congressional races, too. In Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District, both incumbent Republican Brian Fitzpatrick and his Democratic challenger Bob Harvie talked about the need to make childcare more affordable. Fitzpatrick had co-sponsored a number of childcare bills during his five terms in Congress, including the recent Child Care Modernization Act, but ultimately lost the race.   In Georgia, Democratic Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms campaigned on a promise to fulfill the state's universal pre-K goal in part by allowing casino gambling. Ballot measures to fund childcare passed in Boulder County, Colo., and Marin County, Calif.   
   But there were also setbacks for public childcare funding. Voters in St. Louis, Mo., and Tempe, Ariz., rejected sales tax increases intended to raise additional funding for childcare. And childcare advocates say a successful statewide property tax cut in Florida, which is expected to drain local government revenues, will harm programs that support children and families.   Reversing 'attacks' on childcare   Zero to Three's Boteach said she expects the new Democratic majority in Congress to push back on what she called "an attack and a retrenchment on child care" from the Trump administration over the past two years, including an overhaul of Head Start that advocates say will weaken the program and attempts to freeze childcare funding to certain states.   Speaking earlier this year about the changes to Head Start, House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark, who is expected to be the next majority leader, said Democrats would "turn this ship around" if they won back the majority in Congress.   
   "This incoming class is definitely going to put the brakes on that," Boteach said, "and to really be doing a lot more oversight and a lot more pushing of a narrative of why we need greater investments in child care and early education."   Democrats say they'll also pursue new childcare policies, with a particular emphasis on affordability. (Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has said childcare will be one of the party's top five priorities come January.) For example, several incoming Democrats have said they want to expand the Child Tax Credit, which helps families with children lower their tax bills.   It's unclear whether those proposals would have the support of President Trump, who has said he wants to work with Democrats but also that he's willing to veto legislation they send to his desk over the next two years.   "They have not been childcare champions to date," Kashen said of the Trump administration. "That being said, in the past, President Trump has talked about childcare, especially when [his daughter] Ivanka was in the White House back in the day, so I think there's lots of possibilities."

title: Politics chat: Duffy calls for more funding, Democrats plans for accountability
description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy demands more money for the country's air travel control systems. Democrats plan for accountability, but not
body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy demands more money for the country's air travel control systems. Democrats plan for accountability, but not enough of them showed up for an impeachment vote.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  If you were supposed to fly this weekend, our sympathies are with you, given the disruptions caused by Friday's nationwide ground stop. Federal officials say things should be back to normal by the end of today. Speaking to reporters yesterday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said communication systems work by a contractor was the culprit, not new AI tools or a cyberattack.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)SEAN DUFFY: We don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment.RASCOE: And that's where we begin with NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson. Good morning, Mara.MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning.RASCOE: Duffy also laid blame on Congress for not giving the FAA more money for upgrades. He's been trying to get $30 billion for months, but on Friday after the ground stop, he demanded 50 billion. Does this crisis increase the chances that he'll get what he's asking for?LIASSON: Well, that's hard to say. Right now, Republicans, who are in charge of Congress until January, have already approved $12 1/2 billion in that One Big Beautiful Bill for safety upgrades. And ranking Democrats on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee said that the administration has only spent $1 billion of those funds. Meanwhile, the president hasn't spoken publicly or posted about this ground stop or the request for more money.RASCOE: Democrats are also calling for a full investigation into the ground stop, so that's another one to add to a growing list. But on this issue of accountability, Democrats fell short last week when there weren't enough House Democrats on a procedural vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth.LIASSON: That's right, and it wasn't a good look. Eleven Democrats were missing from that vote for various reasons. Several of them have apologized for it. But one thing we've heard in our swing voter focus groups is that voters are worried that Democrats will focus too much effort on investigations and not enough effort on affordability, on bringing prices down.Democratic leaders say they understand voters want them to focus on affordability first. Congressman Jamie Raskin, who will lead a lot of these investigations, says he wants to make a connection between corruption and high prices and also propose legislative fixes for the problems that the investigations uncover. But there are barriers to what Democrats can do with legislation. They don't have a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, and President Trump can still veto any bill that both chambers pass.RASCOE: Before they take charge of Congress, Democrats have to vote on their leadership. So do you think that Hakeem Jeffries is a shoo-in for House speaker or that Chuck Schumer will be the Senate majority leader again? I'm putting you on the spot.LIASSON: Well, there are Democrats who feel neither Jeffries nor Schumer fought as hard as they should have against Trump for the last two years. But it's hard to imagine that Jeffries won't be elected speaker. He just presided over the most dramatic victory Democratic House members have had in a generation. Even if some progressives in the House caucus want someone else, he has a very big majority. And the majority makers were those blue dogs and centrist Democrats that flipped red state seats. They made the majority in the House, not the liberals.RASCOE: Well, what about Schumer?LIASSON: Well, that's a little different. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is challenging Schumer. Some Democratic freshmen say they don't want to support Schumer for majority leader. He represents the Democratic establishment. But to his credit, he did recruit the candidates who won in red states and made the new Senate Democratic majority. And as Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego said, when the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract.RASCOE: And we're still getting results from the election. The big news last week - Mississippi is getting a new Democratic senator.LIASSON: That's right. This is history-making. Scott Colom will be Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. This was a race that was won by several thousand votes, one that surprised a lot of people who thought Mississippi was solidly Republican. Still outstanding is Alaska's Senate race. Democrat Mary Peltola has the lead there, but not enough yet to determine if rank choice voting will be triggered.RASCOE: And President Trump is meeting with Russian President Putin and Chinese President Xi this week on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China. This is coming on the heels of the Nvidia scandal. Do you think that'll come up?LIASSON: The White House says it won't. The White House says Trump is going to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons at the meeting and not bring up former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman who is suspected to be a Chinese spy. The New York Times has reported that Trump was told about this on more than one occasion and did nothing.But this story reminds us that there are members of Congress on both sides of the aisle who believe that there should be tougher restrictions on advanced chips being sold to China. Jensen Huang was against that, and Donald Trump has been more willing to send advanced chips to China than the Biden administration has allowed. So we have to watch for some bipartisan pushback on this.RASCOE: That's NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson. Thank you, Mara.LIASSON: You're welcome.

title: In calling for an end to the Iran War, Vance walks a fine line with Trump
description: A rift is opening up between President Trump and Vice President Vance when it comes to the Iran War. NPR's Ayesha Rascoe talks to Susan Glasser
body:
A rift is opening up between President Trump and Vice President Vance when it comes to the Iran War. NPR's Ayesha Rascoe talks to Susan Glasser, staff writer at the New Yorker.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  The day after Republicans suffered a major defeat in the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance posted a list of what Republicans could do to win back disillusioned voters. No. 1 - end the war in Iran. President Trump said he didn't disagree. But last week he posted, quote, "we don't need a deal with Iran." Instead of focusing on Iran, Trump said he was asking Vance to turn his complete and total attention to corruption and crime in cities and states run by Democrats.Joining us now is Susan Glasser, staff writer at The New Yorker. Thank you so much for joining us.SUSAN GLASSER: Oh, great to be with you.RASCOE: Did you read President Trump's post as a response to Vance's criticism of the war?GLASSER: I mean, not to be too blunt, but basically, you have the president of the United States saying to his own vice president, yeah. You're kind of fired from the most important issue that we have, which is how to resolve this unresolved and unwon conflict in the Middle East. If anything, because of how overwhelming the scale of the Democratic victory was in the elections, we've kind of understated the extent to which it is a remarkable thing to have had Vice President Vance publicly blame the president's top foreign policy priority for that overwhelming defeat. Of course, we know Donald Trump. He's furious about this.RASCOE: When Vance said the war is the problem, one thing that stood out to me is he kind of was talking about it as if he wasn't in the administration. Like, he didn't put himself in it.GLASSER: No. I think the big-picture context here, Ayesha, is clearly that Vice President Vance feels his chances, such as they are, for becoming president after Trump slipping away, largely due to the war. Donald Trump, of course, campaigned in 2024 saying he was the candidate of no new wars. And Vance was specifically selected from what you might call the real MAGA America First wing of the Republican Party.For him, this is even more foundational. His people have gone to great lengths, it seems to me, to put out in news reports that he was against the war from the beginning in the private councils that the president had, even though it has technically been his portfolio since the spring to negotiate an end to the conflict with Iran. Obviously, that has not succeeded. There are very dim prospects for any kind of success in a negotiated peace anytime very soon.I think for Vance, it just underscores the problem that American vice presidents have in general, which is to say it is very, very difficult as an incumbent vice president to win election as president. Only two presidents - George H. W. Bush managed to do this in 1988, after two terms of Ronald Reagan. You have to go all the way back to the 19th century before there's another incumbent vice president who managed the feat.RASCOE: Do you look at this as a breakup between Vance and Trump, maybe emotionally if not publicly?(LAUGHTER)GLASSER: It certainly wouldn't be unprecedented with this particular president, who not only fell out with his first vice president. But, you know, it all ended so badly that they're chanting, hang Mike Pence, because he won't do what Donald Trump wanted him to do on January 6. So the odds, it seems to me, based on Trump's history, were always quite high for JD Vance to have a very difficult time.RASCOE: Would it not be, I guess, the biggest irony if it were to happen that Trump leaves office, and it is up to the next president to deal with this war in the Middle East? Is that not a great irony for the president who was supposed to start no new wars?GLASSER: Absolutely. Not only is it a great irony. I - it's a very real possibility that the Iranians may continue in this nether state over the next couple years. Often, wars and conflicts do end not by the leaders who start them. Because they have so much invested politically and in terms of their own legacy in the conflict, it's harder for them to end wars. So historically, that is an analogy.And I'm mindful of the fact that Donald Trump - you know, he sort of came of age in the 1980s. And that image of Jimmy Carter, for him, was basically the definition of American weakness. And as you know, Donald Trump has almost a - sort of a cult of the idea of strength. So it would be a bitter pill, indeed, for him to swallow if the Iranians did to him some version of what they did to Jimmy Carter, which is to slowly strangle Carter's presidency.RASCOE: That's Susan Glasser. She's a staff writer at The New Yorker. Thank you so much for joining us.GLASSER: Great to be with you.

title: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
description: U.S. President Trump attends a ceremony
body:
U.S. President Trump attends a ceremony in honor of Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery on Nov. 11  in Arlington, Va.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.   The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.   The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.   
   Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.   The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit. Trump said as he left the White House Monday that he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.   Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.   The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.   Trilateral meeting   For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.   "The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.   
   "China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said.   A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization.   "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock.   Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China.   "But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.   Putin, for his part, stands to benefit from a meeting with Trump and Xi, as Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark. Trump has made friendlier moves toward Russia in recent months, siding with Putin and striking a deal to release more Russian oil into the market ahead of the midterm elections.   Trump said last month that he was fine with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not being present at a potential meeting with Putin about the war.   "Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.   A White House official said Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting with Xi and Putin. And there is no plan for Putin and Trump to have a separate meeting.   But Trump said Monday he would be talking about his "favorite subject Ukraine."    
   Kagan said the meeting with Xi, Trump and Putin could end up being on the shorter side if there isn't much all parties are willing to discuss. But at the same time, "I could see this going longer because President Trump likes dealing with Putin and Xi. He sees them as his peers. He sees them as important world leaders," Kagan said.   Either way, a photo of the three leaders meeting together is enough to make headlines.   "That picture alone is going to be worth well over a thousand words," Kagan said.   Busan Agreement   This is the second time Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit – but this year's meeting is notably different from last year's in Busan, South Korea, when tensions between the US and China were fraught amid the escalating trade war.   The meeting in Busan established a sort-of truce between the two countries. The U.S. immediately lowered some tariffs on Chinese goods and China agreed to loosen exports on rare earths. But the execution of the agreement has been spotty.   "There's friction in this truce. It's not smooth, but it's basically functional," Kurt Tong, Managing Partner at The Asia Group, said.   A White House official said the U.S. isn't getting rare earths from China at the pace or level they'd like.   "We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this," they said.   Still, Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration. The two sides will likely agree to the renewal either in Shenzhen or later this year at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami, according to Tong.   Meetings in Manila   Before the president arrives in China, he's holding meetings with several allies in Manila, including a meeting with the other leaders of the Quad nations: India, Japan and Australia.   
   "I think it's quite significant symbolically and politically that the U.S., Australia, Japan and India, the major democracies of Asia and the Pacific, get together… it's especially significant that they're doing it just before the meetings in China," Tong said.   The White House said Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand while in the Philippines.   The opportunity in Manila for Trump is to repair and reinforce relationships with countries like Japan and India, and the host country the Philippines. The ASEAN summit is also the region's first look at the president since his party lost control of Congress and on a global stage, a chance to see what the last two years of Trump's presidency may look like.   "I think the real thing that people will be looking at first is, how does he present himself?" Kagan said. "How does his behaviour towards Modi and towards India change? Those are things people will be looking at very, very closely for clues for what the next two years are likely to be like."   Nvidia fallout   A White House official said they don't expect Trump to raise the issue of Huang's affair and resignation with Xi. The focus of the meeting is about trade, the official said.   Huang resigned last week after admitting the extramarital affair with Alice Huang. Trump administration officials are now facing scrutiny and questions about how much they knew about Huang's affair and how much Huang had access to Trump and his orbit.   Trump reiterated Monday he wasn't sure if Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that he wouldn't mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's CEO.   "I think the main impact is here in the United States, where there are calls for accountability with respect to Mr. Huang's activities with the U.S. government and questions about what happened… the net result of that is to provide a tailwind to persons who are interested in tightening up the technology denial regime toward China," Tong said.   
   Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed last week to appear in front of the Senate Banking Committee to answer further questions. Trump stood by Lutnik on Monday, saying there were differing views on how to treat China in his administration.

schema.headline: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout

title: Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
description: Lindsay Clancy and her attorney Kevin Re
body:
Lindsay Clancy and her attorney Kevin Reddington listen as Judge William Sullivan declares a mistrial at the conclusion of Clancy's  murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Sept. 4.
                
                    Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children.  The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.   There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.   "Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.   In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."   
   Judge Sullivan is expected to preside over the new trial. He oversaw Clancy's murder trial that ended in a mistrial two months ago.   The decision to retry Clancy emerges after the judge denied a request from Clancy's defense team to dismiss the criminal charges against her on double jeopardy grounds.   Clancy's defense has argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her young children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.   Clancy was initially tried on three charges of first-degree murder, one for each of her children. Her case has drawn intense media interest, due to the shocking killings of her young children. And as WBUR has reported, the trial has also sparked conspiracy theories online.   Read WBUR's coverage of this case here.   Mistrial sparked defense motion to dismiss   Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, after five weeks of testimony and seven days of jury deliberations. The jurors, nine women and three men, repeatedly told Sullivan they were deadlocked, unable to reach a unanimous decision. Jurors said a lone juror refused to join 11 others in finding Clancy not guilty of murder.   
   Clancy's defense filed several motions after the mistrial. The first asked the court to issue a "required finding of not guilty," a Massachusetts state law term for instances where judges determine there's insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction. Another focused on the holdout juror, asking the court for an inquiry and to examine their responses to a juror questionnaire and other records. Sullivan denied both of those motions.   When deliberations were dragging out at the end of the trial, Reddington had asked the judge to remove the holdout juror, saying the jury foreperson reported one juror refused to follow the law in regards to reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to dismiss the juror, saying he reaffirmed his instructions with all the jurors about the law.   
   Tragic case highlights postpartum mental health   Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. But her attorneys didn't deny that she killed her three children in January of 2023. Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found strangled in the basement of the home Clancy shared with her then-husband Patrick in Duxbury, Mass., south of Boston.   In court, Clancy's defense argued that she can't be held criminally liable because of her mental state at the time of the killings. Her attorney said Clancy was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, and didn't get adequate mental health help when she sought it out.   "I'm appalled and disgusted," Reddington said of Clancy's medical care, as NPR and WBUR reported. "It's repulsive what happened here."   But prosecutors argued Clancy was mentally capable of committing a premeditated crime, accusing her of sending her husband out on errands so she would be alone with their children. And they raised doubts about Clancy's claims that a voice told her to kill them.   "This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said in her closing statement. "That's a distraction to get you angry and passionate about an important issue, but an issue that's not on trial here."   During the trial, the jury visited the house where the Clancy children died. Their bus route also took them past two places Patrick Clancy visited that evening — a CVS and a takeout restaurant -- before returning home to a horrific scene. Sullivan told the jurors that the visit, called a "view" under Massachusetts state law, was meant to "help you better understand the evidence" by seeing the locations and the house's layout.   Clancy remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital where she's been held for more than three years. She was severely injured by attempts to end her own life, and she used a wheelchair during the trial.   
   Massachusetts' highest court recently reversed a conviction in a separate case involving a mother killing her children – a case that both Cruz, the prosecutor, and Sullivan, the judge, also worked on.   In August, the state Supreme Judicial Court ordered a new trial for Latarsha Sanders, saying Sullivan committed an error in not allowing the jury to see medical records documenting Sanders' mental illness after she was arrested. Sanders was convicted of murder in 2022; she had argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she suffered a psychotic episode.
